source_title: Premium: The Hater's Guide To The Memory Crisis
other_side: Where the edition celebrates the race moving to cost — cheaper tokens, performance-per-dollar charts, a frontier model at a tenth of the price — Zitron, publishing the very same day, argues AI's real cost story runs the other way: AI is making everything more expensive. NVIDIA now takes roughly 65% of the world's high-bandwidth memory, the DRAM triopoly of Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron is repricing at will (Micron's gross margin just hit 84.9%), and the result is 'the single-largest increase in the price of consumer electronics in history'. Cheaper per-token models don't change the physics: debt-funded hyperscaler capex is inflating hardware costs for everyone, and when that capex slows, the memory industry faces a glut — in his words, 'everybody loses, unless the AI bubble continues in perpetuity.'
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is the cost of intelligence — what a unit of AI work actually costs, and who pays it. Both accept the same facts: per-task model prices fell sharply this week (GPT-5.6 near Fable quality at a third of the cost, Muse Spark at a tenth), and memory prices are simultaneously spiking, with the triopoly posting record margins. The empirical question that will resolve is whether the cheap tiers are durable economics or subsidy riding on debt-funded capex; the observable that settles it is whether those advertised prices hold through the next year while DRAM and HBM costs keep rising. The residue is worldview: a maturing industry driving costs down, or a bubble transferring cash to memory-makers. NLW is vindicated if cheap tiers hold and paid adoption grows; Zitron if consumer-electronics inflation persists and a capex slowdown breaks the memory industry. Both are polemicists — NLW sells bullishness, Zitron bubble certainty — so note where they agree: per-task prices are falling while hardware input costs rise. That collision is the story. Watch whether Terra, Luna and Muse Spark hold their launch prices.
